items.title: I can recall that natural plant compounds can contain active ingredients used for medicinal purposes
items.what: Plants produce a range of bioactive compounds including alkaloids, flavonoids and terpenoids that have known medicinal effects on the human body.
items.why: Recognising that medicines can originate from natural sources helps explain why plant extracts have been used historically and why they continue to be investigated in modern pharmaceutical research.
items.example: The Pittosporum angustifolium (gumby gumby) plant contains alkaloids in its leaves that have traditionally been used to treat colds and coughs by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.

subtopic.name: Natural Plant Compounds and Extraction
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how plants produce bioactive compounds such as alkaloids, flavonoids and terpenoids that can be used as medicines. It also covers the laboratory techniques of solvent extraction and distillation used to isolate and purify these compounds.
subtopic.why: Many important medicines, including morphine and quinine, were originally derived from plants. Understanding extraction techniques is essential for obtaining pure, usable compounds from raw plant material for pharmaceutical development.

items.title: I can describe how solvent extraction is used to extract and purify natural plant compounds
items.what: Solvent extraction involves dissolving a desired compound from plant material into a chosen solvent, then separating and removing that solvent to isolate the compound. The solvent is chosen for its selectivity toward the desired compound over impurities.
items.why: Plant material contains many compounds mixed together. Solvent extraction allows chemists to selectively remove the active ingredient from this mixture so it can be used safely and effectively as a medicine.
items.example: Ground gumby gumby leaves are mixed with ethanol, which dissolves the alkaloids. The mixture is filtered, the solvent is evaporated under vacuum to give a crude extract, and the extract is then further separated using a separating funnel with water and an immiscible organic solvent.

items.title: I can describe how distillation is used to extract and purify natural plant compounds
items.what: Distillation separates and purifies compounds based on differences in their boiling points. The component with the lower boiling point vaporises first, travels through a condenser, cools back to liquid and is collected separately.
items.why: When the active compound of interest is a liquid, distillation provides a reliable method for purifying it away from other substances with different boiling points.
items.example: In a simple distillation setup, a plant extract is heated in a round-bottom flask using an oil bath. The compound with the lowest boiling point vaporises first, passes through the condenser where cooling water causes it to condense, and it is collected as a purified distillate in a separate flask.

items.title: I can recall common classes of organic medicines and the key functional groups that characterise each class
items.what: Different classes of medicines are defined by their functional groups: analgesics like aspirin and ibuprofen contain a carboxyl group and benzene ring; opioids like morphine contain hydroxyl, amine and benzene ring; antibiotics like penicillin contain a beta-lactam ring; steroids contain carbonyl and hydroxyl groups.
items.why: Classifying medicines by their functional groups allows chemists and pharmacologists to predict biological activity, design new drugs and understand why structurally related compounds often have similar effects.
items.example: Both aspirin and ibuprofen contain a carboxyl group (–COOH) and a benzene ring. These shared structural features explain why both act as pain-relieving anti-inflammatory agents despite being different molecules.

subtopic.name: Functional Groups in Medicines
subtopic.what: This subtopic examines the key functional groups present in different classes of organic medicines, including analgesics, opioids, antibiotics and steroids. It also explores why functional groups are so important for how medicines work in the body.
subtopic.why: The biological activity of a drug is largely determined by its functional groups, which dictate how it interacts with receptors, enzymes and other biological molecules. Understanding this relationship enables the rational design of new and improved medicines.

items.title: I can explain why understanding functional groups helps guide future drug development
items.what: Functional groups determine how a drug interacts with specific biological targets such as enzymes and receptors. By understanding which functional groups are responsible for a drug's mechanism of action, chemists can modify or replace groups to improve effectiveness, reduce side effects or increase solubility.
items.why: Most new drugs are not discovered by chance but are designed rationally based on existing knowledge of structure-activity relationships. Understanding functional groups is therefore central to modern pharmaceutical development.
items.example: If a drug has a hydroxyl group (–OH) that improves its water solubility and binding to an enzyme, a chemist might replace it with a methyl group (–CH3) to test whether solubility decreases and whether antibacterial activity is lost, thereby confirming the role of that group.

items.title: I can define 'chiral centre' and identify compounds that contain a chiral centre
items.what: A chiral centre is a carbon atom bonded to four different groups. Carbon atoms bonded to fewer than four different groups, those in CH2 or CH3 groups, or those involved in double or triple bonds are not chiral centres.
items.why: Identifying chiral centres is the first step in determining whether a molecule can exist as enantiomers. This has direct implications for how a drug is developed and tested.
items.example: In the molecule 2-butanol (CH3-CHOH-CH2-CH3), carbon 2 is bonded to four different groups: –OH, –H, –CH3 and –CH2CH3. Because all four groups are different, carbon 2 is a chiral centre.

subtopic.name: Chirality and Isomers
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the concept of chirality in organic molecules, how chiral centres are identified, what enantiomers are, and why the presence of different isomers in a medicine can lead to very different biological outcomes.
subtopic.why: Many drug molecules are chiral, meaning they exist as two non-superimposable mirror images. One form may be therapeutic while the other may be inactive or even harmful, as illustrated by the thalidomide tragedy. This makes identifying and controlling chirality critical in drug development.

items.title: I can describe how chiral centres result in isomers and enantiomers
items.what: When a molecule contains a chiral centre, it can exist as two non-superimposable mirror image structures called enantiomers. Enantiomers have the same molecular formula, the same connectivity of atoms, and the same physical properties, but differ in the three-dimensional arrangement of groups around the chiral centre.
items.why: Because biological molecules such as enzymes and receptors are themselves chiral, they may interact differently with each enantiomer. This means the two mirror-image forms of a drug can have entirely different effects in the body.
items.example: Thalidomide has one chiral centre and therefore exists as two enantiomers: R-thalidomide and S-thalidomide. Although their molecular formulas are identical, R-thalidomide acts as a sedative while S-thalidomide causes severe birth defects.

subtopic.name: Chirality and Isomers
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the concept of chirality in organic molecules, how chiral centres are identified, what enantiomers are, and why the presence of different isomers in a medicine can lead to very different biological outcomes.
subtopic.why: Many drug molecules are chiral, meaning they exist as two non-superimposable mirror images. One form may be therapeutic while the other may be inactive or even harmful, as illustrated by the thalidomide tragedy. This makes identifying and controlling chirality critical in drug development.

items.title: I can explain why the presence of isomers in medicines can cause problems
items.what: If a drug is administered as a mixture of enantiomers (a racemic mixture), one enantiomer may be therapeutic while the other is ineffective, toxic or causes harmful side effects. Additionally, some enantiomers can interconvert in the body, making it impossible to administer only the safe form.
items.why: Understanding the potential dangers of racemic mixtures is essential for safe drug development. Modern pharmaceutical practice requires testing each enantiomer separately and, where possible, producing and administering only the active enantiomer.
items.example: When thalidomide was prescribed to pregnant women, it was given as a racemic mixture. Even if only R-thalidomide were administered, the body converts it to the S form, meaning there is no safe way to use thalidomide during pregnancy. This led to thousands of cases of limb malformations.

items.title: I can define the primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary structures of proteins
items.what: Primary structure is the linear sequence of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. Secondary structure involves local folding into alpha helices and beta-pleated sheets. Tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional shape of a single polypeptide chain. Quaternary structure involves two or more polypeptide chains interacting to form a functional protein.
items.why: Each level of protein structure builds on the previous one and ultimately determines the protein's function. Disrupting any level can render the protein non-functional.
items.example: Haemoglobin has a quaternary structure consisting of four polypeptide chains. An antibody also has quaternary structure, consisting of two heavy chains and two light chains held together by disulfide bridges.

subtopic.name: Protein Structure
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the four levels of protein structure — primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary — including the types of bonds and interactions responsible for each level. It also introduces amino acids, peptide bonds and the concept of polypeptide chains.
subtopic.why: Enzymes are proteins, and their ability to function depends entirely on their three-dimensional structure. Understanding protein structure is therefore necessary for explaining how enzymes work, how they can be disrupted, and how medicines can target them.

items.title: I can describe the interactions and bonding important at each level of protein structure
items.what: Primary structure is held by covalent peptide (amide) bonds between amino acids. Secondary structures are held by hydrogen bonds between C=O and N–H groups of the amide backbone. Tertiary and quaternary structures are maintained by hydrogen bonds, ionic interactions, disulfide bridges, hydrophobic interactions and dipole-dipole interactions between R groups.
items.why: The types of bonds at each level determine how stable that structure is and how easily it can be disrupted. Weaker intermolecular forces at the tertiary level are more vulnerable to changes in temperature and pH than the covalent peptide bonds of the primary structure.
items.example: At the tertiary level, two cysteine amino acids can form a covalent disulfide bridge (–S–S–) between their R groups, while two amino acids with charged R groups (like lysine and aspartic acid) can form an ionic interaction.

subtopic.name: Protein Structure
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the four levels of protein structure — primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary — including the types of bonds and interactions responsible for each level. It also introduces amino acids, peptide bonds and the concept of polypeptide chains.
subtopic.why: Enzymes are proteins, and their ability to function depends entirely on their three-dimensional structure. Understanding protein structure is therefore necessary for explaining how enzymes work, how they can be disrupted, and how medicines can target them.

items.title: I can explain how two alpha-amino acids join together to form a peptide bond
items.what: Amino acids join through a condensation reaction in which the carboxyl group of one amino acid reacts with the amine group of another, releasing a water molecule and forming a peptide (amide) bond between them.
items.why: Peptide bonds are the foundation of all protein structure. Every protein in the body is built from amino acids linked in this way, and the sequence of these links defines the protein's identity and function.
items.example: When alanine and glycine react, the –COOH of alanine reacts with the –NH2 of glycine to release one water molecule (H2O) and form a dipeptide connected by a –CO–NH– peptide bond.

items.title: I can recall that enzyme function involves the binding of a substrate to an active site
items.what: An enzyme has a region called the active site with a specific shape and charge complementary to its substrate. The substrate binds to the active site to form an enzyme-substrate complex, lowering the activation energy and allowing the reaction to proceed.
items.why: The active site is the functional core of the enzyme. Its highly specific shape means that each enzyme generally catalyses only one type of reaction with one specific substrate.
items.example: The enzyme HMG-CoA reductase has an active site that is complementary in shape and charge to its substrate HMG-CoA. When HMG-CoA binds to this active site, the enzyme catalyses a reaction that produces cholesterol.

subtopic.name: Enzyme Function and Activity
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how enzymes function as biological catalysts using the lock-and-key model, and how their activity is affected by changes in temperature and pH, including the processes of denaturation and zwitterion formation.
subtopic.why: Enzymes control almost every biochemical process in living organisms. Understanding how they work and how their activity can be altered is fundamental to understanding disease and how many medicines exert their effects.

items.title: I can describe the lock-and-key model of enzyme function
items.what: The lock-and-key model describes how the substrate (the key) has a shape that is complementary to the active site of the enzyme (the lock). The substrate fits precisely into the active site, and this matching of shape and charge allows the enzyme-substrate complex to form and the reaction to take place.
items.why: The lock-and-key model explains enzyme specificity: just as only a specific key fits a specific lock, only a specific substrate fits a specific enzyme's active site. This model also explains how inhibitors can block enzyme activity.
items.example: Neuraminidase on the surface of the influenza virus has an active site shaped specifically to bind its substrate. Relenza is designed to have a complementary shape to this active site, fitting it like a key in a lock and blocking it.

subtopic.name: Enzyme Function and Activity
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how enzymes function as biological catalysts using the lock-and-key model, and how their activity is affected by changes in temperature and pH, including the processes of denaturation and zwitterion formation.
subtopic.why: Enzymes control almost every biochemical process in living organisms. Understanding how they work and how their activity can be altered is fundamental to understanding disease and how many medicines exert their effects.

items.title: I can explain the effect of temperature changes, including denaturation, on enzyme activity
items.what: Below the optimal temperature, enzyme activity increases as temperature rises because molecules have more kinetic energy and collide more frequently and successfully. Above the optimal temperature, the bonds maintaining the tertiary and quaternary structure begin to break, altering the active site's shape so the substrate can no longer bind — this is called denaturation, and it is irreversible.
items.why: Temperature control is critical for enzyme function in living organisms. This explains why fever can be dangerous, as elevated body temperature can begin to denature enzymes, disrupting biochemical processes.
items.example: Most human enzymes have an optimal temperature of around 37°C. At 20°C, enzyme activity is reduced because molecules move slowly. At 60°C, the enzyme denatures: the active site changes shape permanently, and the substrate can no longer bind even if the temperature is later reduced back to 37°C.

subtopic.name: Enzyme Function and Activity
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how enzymes function as biological catalysts using the lock-and-key model, and how their activity is affected by changes in temperature and pH, including the processes of denaturation and zwitterion formation.
subtopic.why: Enzymes control almost every biochemical process in living organisms. Understanding how they work and how their activity can be altered is fundamental to understanding disease and how many medicines exert their effects.

items.title: I can explain the effect of changes in pH on enzyme activity
items.what: Changes in pH alter the ionisation state of the R groups of amino acids within the enzyme. This disrupts the ionic interactions and other bonds that maintain the tertiary and quaternary structure, changing the shape of the active site and reducing enzyme activity. Extreme pH changes can permanently denature the enzyme.
items.why: Different enzymes function at different optimal pH values suited to their location in the body. This explains why pepsin (optimal pH 1.5–2) works in the acidic stomach while salivary amylase (optimal pH 6.5) works in the neutral mouth.
items.example: At low pH, the carboxyl group in the R group of glutamic acid does not ionise and carries no negative charge. This prevents it from forming an ionic interaction with the positively charged amine group of lysine, disrupting the tertiary structure and altering the active site.

subtopic.name: Enzyme Function and Activity
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how enzymes function as biological catalysts using the lock-and-key model, and how their activity is affected by changes in temperature and pH, including the processes of denaturation and zwitterion formation.
subtopic.why: Enzymes control almost every biochemical process in living organisms. Understanding how they work and how their activity can be altered is fundamental to understanding disease and how many medicines exert their effects.

items.title: I can define 'zwitterion' and explain how it forms in relation to amino acids
items.what: A zwitterion is a molecule that carries both a positive and a negative charge simultaneously, giving it an overall neutral charge. In amino acids, the amine group (–NH2) accepts a proton to become –NH3+ and the carboxyl group (–COOH) donates a proton to become –COO–, forming a zwitterion.
items.why: Zwitterion formation explains how changes in pH affect the charge of amino acid R groups, which in turn disrupts the ionic interactions maintaining enzyme structure. This links pH changes directly to loss of enzyme function.
items.example: At neutral pH, aspartic acid exists predominantly as a zwitterion: its amine group carries a positive charge (–NH3+) and its carboxyl group carries a negative charge (–COO–), but the overall charge is zero.

subtopic.name: Enzyme Function and Activity
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how enzymes function as biological catalysts using the lock-and-key model, and how their activity is affected by changes in temperature and pH, including the processes of denaturation and zwitterion formation.
subtopic.why: Enzymes control almost every biochemical process in living organisms. Understanding how they work and how their activity can be altered is fundamental to understanding disease and how many medicines exert their effects.

items.title: I can explain the effect of a competitive inhibitor on the rate of enzyme activity
items.what: A competitive inhibitor is a molecule with a shape and charge complementary to the enzyme's active site. It competes with the substrate for access to the active site. When the inhibitor is bound, the substrate cannot bind and no reaction occurs, reducing the overall rate of enzyme activity.
items.why: Understanding how inhibitors reduce enzyme activity at a molecular level explains both natural regulatory mechanisms in cells and the action of many therapeutic drugs.
items.example: Simvastatin has a shape that closely mimics HMG-CoA, the natural substrate of the enzyme HMG-CoA reductase. When simvastatin occupies the active site, HMG-CoA cannot bind, so the enzyme cannot catalyse cholesterol production, reducing blood cholesterol levels.

subtopic.name: Competitive Inhibition as Medicine
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how competitive inhibitors work by binding to an enzyme's active site in place of the substrate, and how this mechanism has been exploited to develop medicines that treat conditions ranging from high cholesterol to viral infections.
subtopic.why: Competitive inhibition is one of the most important mechanisms by which drugs exert their effects. Understanding it allows students to explain how specific medicines work and why the active site is such a valuable drug target.

items.title: I can describe how competitive inhibition can be used as a treatment approach
items.what: Medicines designed as competitive inhibitors bind to the active site of a target enzyme, preventing the normal substrate from binding and blocking the enzyme's biochemical pathway. This can be used to reduce excess production of a harmful substance, block a pathogen's essential enzyme, or prevent a disease process.
items.why: Competitive inhibition provides a targeted, specific approach to treatment because the inhibitor is designed to fit only one particular enzyme's active site, reducing the likelihood of interfering with other biological processes.
items.example: Relenza (zanamivir) is designed to bind to the active site of neuraminidase on the surface of influenza virus particles. By blocking this enzyme, the virus cannot be released from infected host cells and spread to healthy cells, reducing the severity and duration of influenza illness.
